title: Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes & What Helps
meta_title: Arthritis in Older Adults: What Changes & What Helps
meta_description: Arthritis is more common with age but it is treatable. What changes in later life, from medicines to falls risk and exercise, and what helps most.
excerpt: Arthritis care in later life: getting the cause checked, medicine safety, tailored exercise, falls assessment and when to seek urgent help.

content:
Quick answer: Arthritis is more common in later life, but persistent pain is not something to dismiss as ageing. Treatment depends on the cause, your health and your medicines. Tailored exercise, medication review and help with falls risk can support independence. A hot swollen joint, possible giant cell arteritis or a serious fall needs prompt medical assessment.

Age matters, but it is not a diagnosis

Osteoarthritis becomes more common as people get older, but it is not inevitable and does not always get worse. It involves changes in the joint, including cartilage and bone, rather than simply a fixed amount of wear that exercise uses up. Pain, walking ability, sleep and daily activities matter more to a treatment plan than age alone.

Different conditions need different care. Rheumatoid arthritis can start in later life. Gout is a crystal arthritis associated with raised urate levels; medicines and conditions such as kidney disease can affect risk. Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a separate inflammatory condition that causes pain and stiffness around the shoulders, neck and hips. PMR mainly affects people over 65 and is very rare below 50. Do not assume that all new pain is osteoarthritis.

Get the cause checked

See a GP if pain stops normal activities or sleep, keeps returning or worsening, does not improve after 2 weeks of home care, or your joints are stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking. Persistent joint swelling also needs assessment. NICE NG100 says suspected persistent synovitis needs specialist referral, urgently in specified circumstances such as several joints or the small joints of the hands or feet. Normal inflammation tests or negative rheumatoid-factor tests do not rule out the need for urgent referral.

NICE NG226 supports diagnosing typical osteoarthritis without routine imaging in people aged 45 or over who have activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes. A hot swollen joint, rapid deterioration, an injury or prolonged stiffness may need a different assessment. These criteria guide clinicians; they are not a self-diagnosis checklist.

When to get urgent help

Hot swollen joint: ask for an urgent GP appointment or urgent-care advice if the skin around a painful joint is swollen and hot, or you feel unwell, feverish or shivery. Do not wait for a fever before seeking help. Infection can resemble gout and needs urgent assessment.

Possible giant cell arteritis: a new or severe headache, tender scalp or pain in the jaw when eating or talking needs urgent medical advice, especially if you have PMR. Double vision or other vision problems also need urgent assessment; suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms needs same-day hospital eye assessment. Go to A&E or call 999 if you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes. Do not wait for a routine PMR review.

After a fall: call 999 if you may have injured your head, back, neck or hip, or cannot get up. Go to A&E or call 999 for very bad joint pain after injury, inability to walk or bear weight, a displaced joint or loss of feeling around it. Keep the person warm and comfortable and do not try to lift them yourself. For a less severe fall with pain, possible injury or feeling unwell, get urgent advice.

For urgent non-emergency advice, contact your GP or NHS 111 in England, Scotland or Wales. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or local GP out-of-hours service when the surgery is closed. Use 999 for a life-threatening emergency.

Medicines need an individual review

Ask a pharmacist or prescriber to review your full list, including shop-bought painkillers, supplements and medicines from different clinics. Age is one risk factor, but kidney and liver function, heart disease, stomach ulcers, falls, other conditions and drug interactions all matter. Do not assume everyone needs the same lower dose or blood-test schedule simply because they are older. Monitoring depends on the particular medicine and your health.

  • Osteoarthritis and NSAIDs: NICE recommends offering a topical NSAID for knee osteoarthritis and considering one for other joints. If topical treatment is ineffective or unsuitable, an oral NSAID may be considered after checking stomach, kidney, liver and cardiovascular risks, age and other medicines. Offer gastroprotection, such as a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), while taking an NSAID for osteoarthritis. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. A gel still needs a medicine-safety check.
  • Other painkillers: NICE does not routinely recommend paracetamol or weak opioids for osteoarthritis. Limited short-term use is reserved for specified circumstances when other medicines cannot be used or have not worked. Strong opioids should not be offered for osteoarthritis. Do not stop an existing prescription suddenly; discuss it with your prescriber.
  • Inflammatory arthritis: painkillers do not replace disease-modifying treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. Your specialist should tailor treatment and monitoring rather than withholding effective care on age alone.
  • PMR: prednisolone is the main treatment and is gradually reduced under medical supervision. It may start at a moderate dose, rather than always a low dose. Treatment often lasts 12 months to 2 years. Ask about bone protection and monitoring for problems such as high blood sugar, infection and blood pressure. Do not suddenly stop or change steroids without medical advice.

Exercise for arthritis and exercise to prevent falls

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to your needs, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. Pain can increase initially, but regular exercise can reduce pain and improve function and quality of life over time. Start at a manageable level and build up. Ask for help with new symptoms, a marked deterioration or uncertainty about safety, rather than pushing through severe pain.

Walking, cycling, water-based activity and suitable resistance exercise can all be options. NHS guidance for adults 65 and over is to be active every day, reduce long periods of sitting and work on strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. If you have not exercised for some time or have medical conditions or concerns, speak to a GP about a suitable starting point.

Seated exercise can be a useful way to begin moving, but it is not automatically a complete falls-prevention programme. NICE NG249 says these programmes should be progressive, tailored to the person, delivered by appropriately trained professionals and reviewed regularly. They should address relevant functional skills such as balance, coordination, strength and power. A particular class or exercise is not guaranteed to prevent a fall.

Ask about falls, not just joint pain

Arthritis that affects daily life can contribute to falls risk, but balance, eyesight, footwear, blood pressure, medicines, strength and the home environment may also matter. Tell your GP if you have fallen or are worried about walking or balance.

NICE NG249 covers everyone 65 and over, and people 50 to 64 with factors increasing falls risk. In the community, it recommends a full falls assessment after a fall in the past year if you are living with frailty, needed medical treatment for an injury, lost consciousness, could not get up independently or have had 2 or more falls. A person with a single fall and impaired walking or balance should be offered a falls-prevention exercise programme. Assessment is individual, not a prediction based on an age score.

Support may include medication review, an occupational-therapy home hazard assessment, walking-aid advice, eyesight care and a tailored exercise programme. Local referral and self-referral routes vary. Ask your GP practice or community MSK service what is available; do not assume every area has the same service.

Nutrition, bones and gout

A varied, balanced diet supports general health. Calcium and vitamin D matter for bones. NHS advice is to consider 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily in autumn and winter; people who are not often outdoors, including those who are frail, housebound or in care homes, should take it throughout the year. Other groups may also need it year-round. Ask your clinician about your own needs rather than taking high doses to treat joint pain.

Long-term steroids can increase osteoporosis risk. Ask about fracture-risk assessment and whether bone-protection treatment or a bone-density scan is appropriate. Do not assume everyone needs repeated scans on the same timetable. Vitamin D is for bone and muscle health; NICE NG249 finds insufficient evidence to recommend it specifically to reduce falls.

For gout, NICE NG219 says there is not enough evidence that any specific diet prevents flares or lowers serum urate. Follow a healthy, balanced diet; excess alcohol and excess body weight can worsen symptoms. Diet is not a replacement for discussing urate-lowering treatment. If you are underweight, losing weight without trying, struggling to eat or living with frailty, ask for individual nutrition advice rather than following a weight-loss plan.

Joint replacement and practical support

NICE says not to exclude someone from referral for hip, knee or shoulder replacement because of age, weight, smoking or other health conditions. Referral may be appropriate when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical care is ineffective or unsuitable. Referral is not a promise of an operation: the benefits and individual risks still need discussion.

Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, aids and home adaptations may help with daily tasks. Ask your GP practice or local council about assessment routes. Where useful, involve a relative or carer in planning, with your agreement. The aim is care that fits your priorities, whether that means safer stairs, walking to the shops, sleeping better or managing personal care.

key_takeaways: Persistent joint pain or swelling deserves assessment, not dismissal as ageing.
Exercise and falls prevention should be tailored to your health, abilities and goals.
Medicine review, bone health and urgent warning signs matter; age alone does not exclude joint-replacement referral.
